paragraphs: Selecting papers or grant proposals requires judging quality from imperfect evidence. A fixed ranking can conceal this uncertainty, while introducing randomness does not automatically produce a selection rule suited to its intended goal. This paper develops a framework in which each candidate’s quality is described by an interval, allowing uncertainty and overlapping assessments to enter the decision directly.

The proposed method, MERIT, chooses a randomized selection that maximizes the worst-case expected number of top candidates selected. Its robustness criterion asks how well the selection performs under the least favorable quality assignments consistent with the intervals. The authors provide a polynomial-time algorithm and prove desirable axiomatic properties that existing methods do not guarantee.

Experiments use synthetic peer-review data representing conference and grant-funding settings. MERIT matches existing algorithms’ expected utility under fully probabilistic models and performs better under the paper’s worst-case objective. These findings support a specific benefit: randomness can be designed around an explicit, interpretable protection against uncertainty instead of being introduced through an ad hoc lottery.
neurips-2025-a-principled-approach-to-ra.tldr: MERIT randomizes selection using quality intervals to maximize the worst-case expected number of top candidates chosen.

paragraphs: An organizational chatbot must answer useful questions while respecting who may access each source of information. AC-LoRA addresses this problem by keeping separate LoRA adapters for datasets with different permissions. Each adapter is stored alongside an embedding of the documents used to fine-tune it, linking its learned information to a representation that supports retrieval.

When a query arrives, the system selects adapters using both the user’s permissions and similarity to the query. If it retrieves several adapters, it uses those similarity scores again to combine their responses. The routing mechanism requires no additional training, although the individual adapters are fine-tuned on their respective datasets. This distinction explains the title’s qualified claim of being almost training-free.

The authors build an end-to-end prototype and evaluate it on two datasets. They report performance matching or exceeding leading LoRA mixing techniques while maintaining strong information isolation guarantees. They also show that the design applies across modalities. The contribution combines access-aware selection with useful response generation in one system, rather than treating permissions as separate from adapter retrieval.
neurips-2025-ac-lora-almost-training-fre.tldr: AC-LoRA routes queries to permission-appropriate adapters without additional routing training while maintaining strong information isolation guarantees.

paragraphs: An attention matrix describes how tokens attend to one another. This paper interprets that matrix as a discrete-time Markov chain, turning attention into a process that can propagate through successive token-to-token transitions. The interpretation brings common operations such as selecting, summing, and averaging attention scores into a shared framework while also accounting for indirect connections.

The central observation is that tokens associated with semantically similar regions form metastable states: groups in which attention tends to remain concentrated. Noisy attention scores dissipate through propagation. The authors identify these states using matrix multiplication and assess their prevalence using eigenanalysis. With these lightweight operations, they report state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot segmentation.

The framework also defines TokenRank, a global token-importance measure obtained from the chain’s steady-state vector. The authors show improvements in unconditional image generation, reporting gains in IS and FID, and demonstrate benefits when TokenRank is added to existing segmentation methods. Together, these applications show how following attention beyond immediate links can provide useful information about both semantic regions and overall token importance.
neurips-2025-attention-as-discrete-time-.tldr: Interpreting attention as a Markov chain reveals indirect token relationships that improve segmentation and image generation.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether one architecture is always best for a particular reasoning task. It studies Compositional Reasoning Questions, a family of multistep problems with a tree-like structure, including Boolean formula evaluation. Such problems require combining intermediate results, making them a useful setting for comparing transformers, recurrent neural networks, and transformers that produce chain-of-thought tokens.

Under standard hardness assumptions, the authors prove that none of these architectures can solve the family while keeping its relevant resource fixed as inputs grow. Those resources are transformer depth, recurrent-network embedding dimension, and the number of chain-of-thought tokens. The result is conditional on the hardness assumptions and concerns expressive capability across growing problem sizes.

The paper also constructs solutions: logarithmic depth for transformers, logarithmic embedding dimension for recurrent networks under a specified input ordering, and n chain-of-thought tokens for the third architecture. For recurrent networks with that ordering, logarithmic dimension is both necessary and sufficient. These results show several ways to overcome the problems’ difficulty, with different resource tradeoffs rather than one architecture strictly dominating the others.
neurips-2025-compositional-reasoning-wit.tldr: Tree-structured reasoning requires growing architectural resources, but transformers, RNNs, and chain-of-thought models can meet that demand in different ways.

paragraphs: Methods for explaining time-series predictions often alter selected portions of a signal and observe how the prediction changes. Most such methods assume regularly spaced measurements. Contimask addresses irregular records, where measurement times vary and values may be absent. In these settings, the pattern of observation itself can carry information that an explanation based only on recorded values would overlook.

The authors first translate existing techniques into continuous time and examine the circumstances in which they remain applicable. They then introduce a framework supporting perturbations that need not be differentiable. Using NeuroEvolution, Contimask can simulate parts of a record never having been observed, allowing explanations to probe the role of observation structure as well as signal content.

On a real-world sepsis prediction task with 90% missing data, the method detects how structural differences in the records can bias model predictions. The finding matters because missingness may be informative rather than random. An explanation can therefore reveal sensitivity to how data were collected, extending the usual question of which measured values influenced a prediction.
neurips-2025-contimask-explaining-irregu.tldr: Contimask explains irregular time-series predictions by perturbing observation patterns as well as recorded data.

paragraphs: Vaccination strategies can use a contact network to identify interventions that limit epidemic spread, particularly when vaccines are scarce. The challenge is greater when contacts are distributed unevenly across people. Network properties such as maximum degree and spectral radius provide useful control targets, but selecting interventions around them requires information about potentially sensitive interpersonal contacts.

This paper develops vaccination algorithms with differential privacy guarantees for network edges. The algorithms aim to reduce maximum degree and spectral radius while protecting the contact information used in their decisions. Their central technical component is a private algorithm for a combinatorial problem called multi-set multi-cover, which the authors use to control those network properties.

The evaluation examines privacy-utility tradeoffs on both synthetic and real-world networks and reports effective strategies. The contribution connects two requirements that must be handled together: exploiting contact structure to guide vaccination and limiting what the selection process reveals about that structure. Its stated privacy protection concerns edges, matching the paper’s focus on sensitive relationships within the network.
neurips-2025-controlling-the-spread-of-e.tldr: The paper develops differentially private vaccination algorithms that reduce network properties associated with epidemic spread while protecting contact edges.

paragraphs: EA3D builds a geometric and semantic understanding of a scene as video frames arrive. This addresses a restriction of approaches that depend on previously collected views or an already constructed 3D representation. The framework combines object extraction with reconstruction, so information about what objects are and how they occupy space develops within the same online process.

For each frame, vision-language and 2D vision encoders extract object-level information. EA3D incorporates this information into a Gaussian feature map through feed-forward updates. It also estimates camera motion from historical frames and adds new observations incrementally. A recurrent joint optimization module focuses on regions of interest while improving geometry and semantic understanding together.

Experiments cover photorealistic rendering, semantic and instance segmentation, 3D bounding boxes, semantic occupancy estimation, and mesh generation. The reported effectiveness across these tasks supports the value of a shared representation for several scene-understanding outputs. The central contribution is a unified, efficient online framework in which streaming observations continuously refine both the reconstructed scene and its object-level interpretation.
neurips-2025-ea3d-online-open-world-3d-o.tldr: EA3D incrementally combines streaming video observations into a shared representation for 3D reconstruction and object-level scene understanding.

paragraphs: Event cameras supply fine-grained timing information that can help generate frames between existing video frames. Yet fast motion and occlusion can leave both input frames and training targets blurred or distorted. EPA addresses the resulting supervision problem: directly matching degraded images can interfere with learning interpolated frames that look perceptually realistic across different scenes.

The method builds on the observation that degradation changes semantic-perceptual representations less than it changes images at the pixel level. Its first phase combines a DINO-based perceptual extractor, a customized style adapter, and a reconstruction generator to obtain features at several levels that are relatively insensitive to degradation. These features provide the learning signals.

A second component, Bidirectional Event-Guided Alignment, uses event timing and deformable convolutions to align perceptual features between keyframes and target frames. This reduces dependence on direct image-level supervision and improves robustness to degraded inputs and unreliable targets. Experiments report interpolated frames that better match human perceptual preferences, supporting the use of semantic-perceptual learning signals when the available imagery is imperfect.
neurips-2025-epa-boosting-event-based-vi.tldr: EPA uses degradation-insensitive perceptual supervision and event-guided alignment to produce more perceptually realistic interpolated video frames.

paragraphs: Learning in a recurrent neural network requires assigning responsibility for errors across activity that unfolds over time. This paper explores how feedback can directly guide neural activity during learning, addressing known difficulties with backpropagation through time. Its central question is how to use corrective feedback effectively without imposing unnecessarily strong constraints on the network’s evolving dynamics.

The proposed method, error forcing, guides activity orthogonally toward the zero-error manifold: the set of activity configurations associated with zero error. This geometric rule specifies the direction of correction. Compared with alternatives that more strongly prescribe neural activity, the method exerts less feedback influence on circuit dynamics. The authors also interpret it as approximate dynamic inference from a Bayesian perspective.

Across several tasks, error forcing consistently outperforms the other learning algorithms evaluated. Its benefits remain when additional biological constraints are included. These results support error forcing as a temporal credit-assignment mechanism and a promising candidate model for biological learning. The biological connection is a proposed modeling role, supported by those constrained evaluations.
neurips-2025-error-forcing-in-recurrent-.tldr: Error forcing improves recurrent-network learning by directing neural activity toward zero-error configurations with comparatively restrained feedback.

paragraphs: Vision-language encoders assign similarity scores to images and text, supporting tasks such as retrieval and zero-shot classification. Explaining those scores requires understanding how the two inputs work together. Common saliency methods assign importance to individual input components, which can overlook cross-modal interactions that contribute to the model’s judgment.

FIxLIP decomposes similarity using a game-theoretic interaction framework. It uses weighted Banzhaf interactions to provide greater flexibility and computational efficiency than the Shapley interaction framework considered in the paper. By examining second-order contributions, the method can explain joint effects instead of limiting the analysis to separate importance scores. This makes interaction itself part of what the explanation represents.

The authors also extend explanation-evaluation tools, including the pointing game and insertion/deletion-based measures, to assess second-order explanations. Experiments on MS COCO and ImageNet-1k show second-order methods such as FIxLIP outperforming first-order attribution methods. The paper further demonstrates comparisons between CLIP and SigLIP-2, showing that interaction explanations can help characterize differences between models as well as explain individual similarity outputs.
neurips-2025-explaining-similarity-in-vi.tldr: FIxLIP explains image-text similarity through cross-modal interactions and outperforms first-order attribution methods on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: A trained image classifier can be difficult to modify when a class should be forgotten or its operating environment changes. This paper introduces class vectors as a way to describe and manipulate class-specific adaptation. They capture adjustments in the model’s internal representations during fine-tuning, separating the changes associated with individual classes.

The distinction from task vectors is where and at what level changes are represented: task vectors describe task-wide weight changes, whereas class vectors describe class-level changes in latent space. The authors show two ways to use them for editing. One steers internal features along the vectors; the other maps the vectors into weight space to change decision boundaries.

The paper also finds linearity and orthogonality properties that support combining class vectors through simple arithmetic for higher-level concept edits. It demonstrates uses in unlearning, environmental adaptation, adversarial defense, and adversarial trigger optimization. Together, these results present class-specific representation changes as practical editing tools, offering more targeted flexibility than treating every modification as an undifferentiated change to the whole task.
neurips-2025-exploring-and-leveraging-cl.tldr: Class vectors capture class-specific representation changes that can be combined and applied to edit trained image classifiers.

paragraphs: Corrective feedback should help a language model repair an incorrect answer, but how completely does the model use that feedback? This paper investigates the question in a controlled setting. A solver attempts a problem, a feedback generator with access to nearly complete ground-truth answers supplies targeted guidance, and the solver then tries again.

Across mathematics, knowledge reasoning, scientific reasoning, and broader evaluations, the tested models consistently fail to fully incorporate feedback even under these favorable conditions. The authors call this behavior feedback friction. Their evaluation includes state-of-the-art models such as Claude 3.7 with extended thinking, showing that the observed difficulty also appears in advanced reasoning systems.

The authors test progressively increasing sampling temperature and explicitly rejecting earlier incorrect answers. Both strategies help, but they do not bring models to the target performance. Confidence measured through semantic entropy predicts resistance: highly confident predictions are harder to correct. The findings identify feedback uptake as a distinct obstacle to improvement, since providing strong corrective information does not ensure that the solver will use it successfully.
neurips-2025-feedback-friction-llms-stru.tldr: Tested language models resist even highly informative corrections, with greater confidence predicting stronger feedback resistance.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several representations of the same data. Many existing methods emphasize pairwise relationships, potentially overlooking structure shared by larger groups of samples. HOPER addresses this by constructing a separate hypergraph for each view, where a hyperedge can represent a relationship involving multiple samples at once.

A hypergraph neural network learns representations from those structures. The framework then combines two contrastive learning mechanisms: one encourages consistency across views, while the other operates within hyperedges to maintain discriminability. This combination gives the model a way to use group-level relationships without abandoning the distinctions needed to form useful clusters.

HOPER also includes hyper-Laplacian manifold regularization to preserve each view’s local geometric structure. The learning process therefore considers cross-view agreement, higher-order relationships, and local organization together. Experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is the joint treatment of these forms of structure, addressing the possibility that pairwise comparisons alone leave useful information out of the learned representations.
neurips-2025-hypergraph-enhanced-contras.tldr: HOPER combines hypergraphs, contrastive learning, and geometric regularization to capture group-level structure in multi-view clustering.

paragraphs: Physical systems often evolve across widely separated spatial and temporal scales. Simulating every relevant detail requires a fine discretization and a large state space, which makes computation expensive. This paper learns stochastic differential-equation models directly from observations, aiming to retain useful fine-scale dynamics while representing the observable large-scale state on a coarse mesh.

The model includes a latent microscale state that explicitly describes dynamics unresolved by that mesh. Its parameters are learned through simulator-free amortized variational inference. A Product of Experts likelihood enforces separation between scales, making scale separation part of the learning formulation. The coarse and latent states together provide the multiscale description.

Detailed numerical studies report better predictive accuracy than under-resolved direct simulations and closure-type models at equivalent resolution, as well as reduced-order modeling approaches. These comparisons support the benefit of learning an explicit representation of unresolved dynamics. The result is a data-driven route to multiscale prediction in which coarse resolution need not mean discarding all information about the smaller-scale processes influencing the system.
neurips-2025-learning-stochastic-multisc.tldr: The method learns stochastic models that combine coarse physical states with latent fine-scale dynamics to improve prediction.

paragraphs: Reasoning segmentation identifies objects according to a person’s intent and spatial descriptions. MLLM-For3D transfers this capability from 2D multimodal language models to 3D scenes. It generates segmentation masks and text embeddings from multiple views, projects those masks into 3D, and aligns the resulting object information with the text representations.

This transfer creates a specific challenge: individual views lack full 3D context. Their predictions can include nonexistent objects or refer inconsistently to the target across views. MLLM-For3D filters irrelevant views using token attention, then applies a token-for-Query alignment approach to support consistent identification of the same object. A spatial consistency strategy further encourages the masks to agree within the scene’s 3D geometry.

On challenging indoor-scene benchmarks, the framework outperforms existing 3D reasoning segmentation methods without labeled 3D training data. The results show that 2D-generated supervision can support 3D intent understanding and spatial reasoning when unreliable views and cross-view inconsistencies are addressed. Those corrective steps are central to making the transferred supervision useful.
neurips-2025-mllm-for3d-adapting-multimo.tldr: MLLM-For3D turns filtered, spatially consistent 2D model predictions into supervision for 3D reasoning segmentation without labeled 3D training data.

paragraphs: Kernel-based methods can learn solutions to ordinary differential equations, but their computational cost becomes prohibitive as the number of time points grows. For the least-squares support vector machine formulation studied here, a major cost term grows cubically with that number. This paper restructures the problem so that the equation systems depend on a chosen feature dimension.

The method derives an explicit Nyström feature mapping and its derivatives, then expresses the differential equations as constraints in primal feature space. The feature count m can be smaller than the number of time points n. This makes it possible to work with many temporal samples while solving systems whose complexity depends on the smaller representation.

Across sixteen benchmark equations, the authors report computation 10–6000 times faster than classical LS-SVMs and physics-informed neural networks, with accuracy comparable to LS-SVMs. They also report improvements over PINNs reaching 72% in RMSE and demonstrate 10,000 time steps using 50 features. These results show a substantial empirical efficiency gain without a significant loss of solution accuracy.
neurips-2025-nystrom-accelerated-primal-.tldr: A Nyström feature-space reformulation accelerates kernel-based ODE learning while retaining accuracy comparable to classical LS-SVMs.

paragraphs: One-shot visual imitation asks a robot to learn what to do from a single demonstration video without additional fine-tuning. Generalizing to unseen tasks is difficult because visually similar situations can require different actions when their context or structure changes. OSVI-WM addresses this challenge by explicitly modeling how the environment evolves during the proposed behavior.

Given the demonstration and the robot’s initial observation, a learned world model predicts a sequence of latent states and actions. The system then decodes this trajectory into physical waypoints that guide execution. This provides a representation of future states between observing the expert and acting, directly addressing the absence of explicit environment dynamics in many existing methods.

The authors evaluate the framework on two simulated benchmarks and three real-world robotic platforms. It consistently outperforms prior approaches in those evaluations, with improvements exceeding 30% in some cases. The findings support world-model-guided trajectory generation as a useful approach to transferring a demonstrated task to the agent’s own situation, including tasks with unfamiliar semantic or structural requirements.
neurips-2025-osvi-wm-one-shot-visual-imi.tldr: OSVI-WM uses a learned world model to turn one demonstration into a predicted trajectory and executable robotic waypoints.

paragraphs: A human intervention tells an agent that its current behavior needs correction, but the information may also be useful for states it will encounter next. Predictive Preference Learning from Human Interventions uses that implicit preference to train on predicted future states. The aim is to extend the value of each correction into potentially hazardous regions ahead.

The method propagates an intervention over a preference horizon of L future steps. It assumes that the agent repeats the same action and the human supplies the same intervention throughout that horizon. Preference optimization then applies the resulting corrections to those future states. This assumption is central because it determines when the projected preference labels remain appropriate.

Experiments in autonomous driving and robotic manipulation demonstrate improved learning efficiency and reduced need for human demonstrations. The theoretical analysis explains the tradeoff in choosing L: a longer horizon covers more risky states, while label correctness must also be maintained. Selecting an appropriate horizon balances these effects and bounds the algorithmic optimality gap.
neurips-2025-predictive-preference-learn.tldr: PPL extends human corrections into predicted future states, balancing broader risk coverage against the reliability of projected preference labels.

paragraphs: PurpCode is a post-training approach for coding models that combines two safety goals: producing secure code and avoiding assistance with malicious cyberactivity. It also seeks to preserve useful coding and security capabilities. The approach explicitly trains reasoning around cybersafety rules, making those rules part of how the model learns to respond.

Training has two stages. Rule Learning teaches the model to reference safety rules when generating code and deciding how to handle harmful requests. Reinforcement Learning then uses multiple reward objectives to improve safety while retaining utility. The authors support this process with synthesized prompts developed through internal red-teaming and grounded in real-world tasks.

Using this recipe, they produce PurpCode-32B and report state-of-the-art cybersafety performance, exceeding various frontier models in their evaluation. They also report lower overrefusal rates in both general and cybersecurity-specific settings while preserving code-generation ability and common security knowledge. These findings matter because the stated gains combine stronger safety with fewer unnecessary refusals, rather than measuring safety solely through a model’s willingness to decline requests.
neurips-2025-purpcode-reasoning-for-safe.tldr: PurpCode combines safety-rule learning and multi-objective reinforcement learning to improve coding-model cybersafety while reducing overrefusal.

paragraphs: Single-step retrosynthesis predicts reactants that could produce a desired molecule. The search is combinatorial, and a useful model must offer plausible alternatives while making accurate predictions. RETRO SYNFLOW formulates this task through discrete flow matching, using a Markov bridge to connect the product molecule with candidate reactants.

The framework first identifies a reaction center and extracts intermediate structures called synthons. These give the flow model a more structured starting distribution. During generation, Feynman-Kac steering and Sequential Monte Carlo resampling guide candidates using a learned forward-synthesis reward model. This adds a mechanism for favoring reactants whose predicted forward behavior is promising while supporting diversity.

Empirically, the method substantially improves top-1 accuracy over previous leading approaches. The steering component also significantly improves round-trip accuracy while preserving competitive top-k performance. Round-trip evaluation checks whether proposed reactants lead back toward the target under forward prediction, so the reported gains support stronger chemical validity and synthetic feasibility. The contribution combines reaction-centered structure with guided sampling in a single-step prediction framework.
neurips-2025-retro-synflow-discrete-flow.tldr: RETRO SYNFLOW combines structured reaction intermediates with guided discrete flow generation to improve single-step reactant prediction.

paragraphs: Thompson Sampling balances exploiting promising actions with exploring uncertain ones, but implementing it can be expensive in large or complex settings. Ensemble approximations can help, yet may require many members. Ensemble++ proposes a shared-factor ensemble architecture with random linear combinations to make this form of exploration more computationally practical.

For linear bandits, the authors prove regret comparable to exact Thompson Sampling using an ensemble size of order d log T. The guarantees apply to both compact and finite action sets, with either fixed or changing contexts, without changing the configuration. This gives the method a theoretical basis across several versions of the linear decision problem.

The framework extends to nonlinear rewards by replacing fixed features with learned neural representations while retaining the same incremental update principle. Experiments span linear, quadratic, neural, and GPT-based contextual bandits and report a better regret-computation tradeoff than leading alternatives. The linear guarantees and broader empirical results together support efficient exploration, with the theoretical claim specifically established for the linear setting.
neurips-2025-scalable-exploration-via-en.tldr: Ensemble++ makes exploration more efficient through shared ensemble factors, with linear-bandit guarantees and favorable empirical regret-computation tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Training loss does not fully describe how language-model capabilities emerge. This paper examines the geometry of internal representations using effective rank and eigenspectrum decay. Across OLMo and Pythia models, it identifies three recurring phases during pretraining, revealing changes in how representations use their available dimensions.

An initial warmup phase rapidly collapses representations. An entropy-seeking phase then expands dimensionality and coincides with peak n-gram memorization. Finally, a compression-seeking phase concentrates variation along dominant directions while shrinking others, alongside substantial downstream performance improvement. The authors show that these phases can arise from cross-entropy optimization with uneven token frequencies and representation dimensions much smaller than the vocabulary.

Post-training produces related but distinct changes. In the study, supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization expand representations, improving in-distribution performance while weakening out-of-distribution robustness. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards instead encourages compression, improving reward alignment while reducing generation diversity. These findings connect training choices to representation geometry and behavioral tradeoffs, providing a view of model development beyond the loss curve.
neurips-2025-tracing-the-representation-.tldr: Representation geometry reveals three pretraining phases and distinct post-training tradeoffs involving performance, robustness, reward alignment, and diversity.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate high-quality samples through repeated computation, motivating distillation into a generator that operates in one step. Variational Score Distillation provides one route, but its student update requires the score of the student’s own noisy distribution. Approximating that quantity can introduce bias, destabilize training, or leave aspects of the target distribution unmatched.

VarFlow changes the matching objective. Within a Score-Rule Variational Distillation framework, it minimizes an energy distance between the student’s noisy output distribution and the teacher’s target noisy distribution. The distance comes from a strictly proper energy score and is estimated using samples from the two distributions. This removes the need to compute or approximate the intractable student score.

The intended benefit is broader distributional alignment through a directly sample-estimated objective. Instead of relying on an auxiliary approximation of the student score, the method targets the full noisy marginal distributions. The paper presents this as a theoretically grounded route toward robust, high-fidelity one-step generation; the abstract frames those generation benefits as the method’s aim rather than reporting a quantified empirical gain.
neurips-2025-varflow-proper-scoring-rule.tldr: VarFlow trains a one-step generator through sample-based energy matching that avoids estimating the student distribution’s score.

paragraphs: Transformers trained on algorithmic problems can spend a long time on a performance plateau before suddenly improving. This paper investigates what develops during that apparently stagnant period, primarily in shallow transformers. It finds that models often already possess an interpretable partial solution even while their outputs show a strong tendency to repeat.

That repetition accompanies representation collapse: hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel. The authors identify slow progress toward suitable attention maps as a key bottleneck. Attention configuration continues to improve during the plateau before rapid convergence becomes visible. Direct interventions on attention substantially change plateau length, repetition bias, and the severity of representation collapse.

The study also observes repetition bias and representation collapse during early pretraining of Pythia and OLMo, showing that these two phenomena extend beyond the algorithmic setups. The findings explain how meaningful internal progress can coexist with little visible improvement in the training curve. They also give attention learning a concrete role in the abrupt transitions studied, supported by interventions that alter the dynamics.
neurips-2025-what-happens-during-the-los.tldr: During apparent learning plateaus, transformers can develop partial solutions while slow attention learning, repetition, and representation collapse delay visible progress.

paragraphs: A visually convincing generated video may still be unsuitable as a model of how the world behaves. WorldModelBench evaluates video generators with decision-making applications in mind, adding instruction-following and physics-adherence dimensions to assessment. These dimensions target subtle world-modeling violations that general video-quality benchmarks can overlook.

The benchmark uses 67,000 crowdsourced human labels to evaluate 14 frontier models. The authors also train a 2-billion-parameter judge on these annotations to automate evaluation. They report 9.9% lower error than GPT-4o when predicting world-modeling violations. This makes human assessments useful both as benchmark evidence and as training data for a specialized evaluator.

The paper further uses the judge’s rewards to train generation models toward agreement with human annotations and reports noticeable improvement in world-modeling capability. The contribution therefore connects assessment with a possible improvement mechanism. Its central message is that judging a video generator as a world model requires attention to instructions and physical behavior, because visual quality alone does not capture the capabilities needed for the applications considered.
neurips-2025-worldmodelbench-judging-vid.tldr: WorldModelBench evaluates video generators for instruction following and physical consistency, using human labels and a specialized automated judge.
